solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Angered? Explosively?

indicators.note: Something that goes off explosively ends up in pieces.

blocks.note: The fodder is the clue's own first word.

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person was angry, and whether the anger burst out.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word works twice: it is both the meaning and the letters, and ENRAGED is an exact rearrangement of ANGERED.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: angered and enraged both mean made furious, and the anagram shows the anger bursting out.

clue.text: Defenceless old flame, model, died

blocks.note: A former partner is an ex.
To model for an artist is to pose.
D is the standard abbreviation for died.

explanation.surface: A tragic list of facts about a former lover who modelled and then died, left without protection.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces simply follow the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: Something exposed is open to attack, so defenceless.

clue.text: Publish charter again?

blocks.note: RE- is the prefix meaning again.
To charter a boat or plane is to lease it.

explanation.surface: A question about whether a document or charter should be published a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as RE-LEASE: to charter again. The pieces come in the reverse of the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from publishing: a label or publisher putting out a new title is making it public.

clue.text: Individual in Greece: person with no future

blocks.note: GR is the international vehicle code for Greece.
An individual is one.

explanation.surface: A gloomy description of someone in Greece whose prospects have run out.
explanation.walkthrough: GR is the country code seen on cars from Greece.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal idiom: someone written off as doomed, beyond saving, has no future left.

clue.text: Black inside, rotten old wheat in lethal buffet

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils.

explanation.surface: Someone finds rotten old wheat with something black inside it and suffers a deadly blow from it.
explanation.walkthrough: "old" is not an abbreviation here; its letters are part of the fodder, and B slots in between DEATH and LOW.
explanation.definitionFit: A buffet is a knock or blow, and one that kills is the final, fatal stroke.

clue.text: Drum roll precedes result in this lottery

blocks.note: reads as the drumroll before a winner is announced; the setter means the drum of tickets being turned before one is drawn
the kind of lottery where that drum literally rolls

explanation.surface: The drumroll builds suspense before a lottery winner is announced.
explanation.walkthrough: "Drum roll" sounds like the build-up before an announcement, but in a tombola the prize tickets sit in a revolving drum that is literally rolled before a ticket is drawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A tombola is a raffle-style lottery with tickets drawn from a spinning drum, common at British fêtes.

clue.text: Short story being broadcast — it could be gripping!

blocks.note: A story is a tale, docked to TAL.
A programme being broadcast is on.

explanation.surface: A short story is read out on the radio and promises to be gripping.
explanation.walkthrough: "Short story" reads as a literary genre, and "gripping" as exciting; really it is a clipped TALE, and a talon literally grips.
explanation.definitionFit: A talon is a bird's claw, something that grips.

clue.text: Fellow worker the French treat roughly

blocks.note: A fellow is a man.
A farm or factory worker is a hand.
LE is French for the.

explanation.surface: A complaint that a colleague and the French handle something roughly.
explanation.walkthrough: "Fellow worker" looks like a single phrase meaning colleague; split it into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: shoving or grabbing someone physically is handling them roughly.

clue.text: Butcher to carve ham

indicators.note: To butcher something is to hack it about.

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: Instructions to a butcher about carving a ham.
explanation.walkthrough: The butcher and ham are all meat; "ham" is really a verb for bad acting.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatrical sense: a ham actor exaggerates every gesture, so to ham it up is to act too much.

clue.text: Appeal upheld by an old church in ancient city

indicators.note: In a down clue, holding something up turns it upward.

blocks.note: Taken as printed.
IT is sex appeal.
O is the abbreviation for old.
CH is the abbreviation for church.

explanation.surface: An appeal is backed by an old church in some ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: Appeal as IT, meaning sex appeal, is an old usage worth knowing; in a down clue "upheld" means written upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Antioch was an ancient city in what is now Turkey.

clue.text: Italian dish on plate that’s broken

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: An Italian meal is served on a cracked plate.
explanation.walkthrough: "on" belongs to the fodder, not a positional instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this cornmeal porridge from northern Italy is one of many regional Italian dishes.

clue.text: Mild Russian leader embracing Eastern Time

blocks.note: Lenin led Soviet Russia.
E is the abbreviation for Eastern.
T is the abbreviation for time.

explanation.surface: A gentle Russian leader embracing a new time zone.
explanation.walkthrough: "Eastern Time" reads as a time zone, but it splits: only E goes inside LENIN, and T follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Lenient means mild or gentle in judgement.

clue.text: Look round posh home for creature under shell

blocks.note: To look for something is to search.
U means upper-class, posh.
To be home is to be in.

explanation.surface: Someone looks around an upmarket house for an animal hiding under a shell.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class, posh, is a crossword convention from the old U and non-U debate.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea urchin is a spiny sea creature living inside a round shell.

clue.text: Mission accomplished — like another mission — on all fronts?

indicators.note: The front of every word is taken, so the initials are kept.

blocks.note: The first letter of accomplished.
The first letter of like.
The first letter of another.
The first letter of the second mission.
The first letter of on.

explanation.surface: A military report announces a mission completed, compared with another campaign, across every front.
explanation.walkthrough: "on all fronts" sounds like a battle report; it tells you to take the fronts, the first letters, of the words from accomplished to on.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alamo was a Spanish mission in Texas, famous for its 1836 siege.

clue.text: King had this made afresh to accommodate Republican

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.
R is the abbreviation for Republican.

explanation.surface: A monarch had something rebuilt to house a Republican.
explanation.walkthrough: "King" looks like a monarch, which clashes with a Republican; it is Martin Luther King, who said "I have a dream".
explanation.definitionFit: Martin Luther King's famous 1963 speech declared "I have a dream".

clue.text: Bottom oar disintegrated in seagoing craft

indicators.note: Something that has disintegrated has fallen to bits.

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.

explanation.surface: The lowest oar in a boat at sea falls apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is itself a craft with no oars at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A motorboat is a powered boat that can go to sea.

clue.text: Desperate to survive drop

blocks.note: To last is to survive.
To drop something is to ditch it.

explanation.surface: Someone desperate to survive a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: "Desperate to survive" reads as one phrase, but the definition stops at "Desperate".
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from warfare: defenders making a final stand in the last trench before defeat are desperate.

clue.text: Small offence importing glossy handbags?

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small.
An offence is a crime.
A glossy is a magazine, a mag.

explanation.surface: A petty crime of smuggling shiny designer handbags.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, handbags is a scuffle with more posturing than punches, as between footballers; the question mark flags this sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrimmage is a confused scuffle, which is what handbags means.

clue.text: Is it here one may expect high tolls?

blocks.note: reads as a motorist asking about a spot on the road; the setter means a building
sounds like steep charges at a toll booth; it is bells tolling high above the ground

explanation.surface: A driver asks whether this is the place with expensive road tolls.
explanation.walkthrough: "High tolls" suggests expensive road charges; it is the tolling of bells, up high.
explanation.definitionFit: Bells are rung, or tolled, high up in a bell tower.

clue.text: Will one lying find such support close by?

blocks.note: reads as a liar; the setter means someone lying in bed
sounds like backing for a lie; it is a post holding up the bed right beside the sleeper

explanation.surface: A cynical question whether a liar will find supporters nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: "One lying" suggests a liar looking for backing; it is simply someone lying in bed, next to a bedpost.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedpost is an upright support at the corner of a bed, right beside whoever lies in it.

clue.text: Genial Dicky initially enjoyed descent

blocks.note: Part of the anagram fodder, taken as printed.
The first letter of enjoyed.

explanation.surface: A friendly man called Dicky had fun on the way down a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name; it is British slang for unsound or wobbly, as in a dicky heart.
explanation.definitionFit: Lineage is line of descent, one's ancestry.

clue.text: Regularly behind peers — feel down about this?

indicators.note: Taking letters at regular intervals keeps every second one.

blocks.note: The second, fourth and sixth letters of behind.
The second and fourth letters of peers.

explanation.surface: Someone always lagging behind their peers wonders whether to feel depressed about it.
explanation.walkthrough: "feel down" means feel sad on the surface, but here it means to touch down, the soft feathers the eider is famous for.
explanation.definitionFit: The eider is a sea duck whose soft breast feathers give eiderdown.

clue.text: Olympians in southeast one chained up

indicators.note: In a down clue, going up means reading bottom to top, so the whole string is reversed.

blocks.note: SE is the compass abbreviation.
I is the Roman numeral for one.
Chained means tied.

explanation.surface: Greek gods are found in the southeast, with one of them bound in chains.
explanation.walkthrough: The chained one recalls Prometheus, chained to a rock, but the whole string SEITIED is simply read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The Olympians were the gods of Mount Olympus, so deities.

clue.text: Romeo for example, on the wagon, seen in AA meeting

blocks.note: Romeo is R in the NATO alphabet.
EG abbreviates the Latin for for example.
Taken as printed, and split around TT.
TT means teetotal, and someone on the wagon has given up drink.

explanation.surface: Romeo, now sober, shows up at an Alcoholics Anonymous meeting as an example.
explanation.walkthrough: The AA meeting is the obvious picture, but "meeting" alone is the definition and AA just supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a series of boat races is a sporting meeting on the water.

clue.text: One keen to eat arrested in Erith stores

indicators.note: The phrase stores the answer, keeping it inside.

blocks.note: arresteD IN ERith.

explanation.surface: A hungry person is arrested inside some shops in Erith.
explanation.walkthrough: Erith is a town in south-east London. "arrested in" looks like a container, but the answer runs across the words.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain sense: a person sitting down at a restaurant table is there because they want to eat.

clue.text: Meat and fibre in hamper

blocks.note: Ham is a meat.
String is fibre.

explanation.surface: Meat and fibre packed into a picnic hamper.
explanation.walkthrough: "hamper" looks like a picnic basket; it is the verb meaning to hinder.
explanation.definitionFit: A figurative sense: cutting the tendon behind the knee cripples an animal, so the word came to mean hinder.

clue.text: Astronomer Fred needs year inside crater

blocks.note: A crater is a hole.
Y is the abbreviation for year.

explanation.surface: An astronomer needs a year inside a lunar crater to study it.
explanation.walkthrough: Fred Hoyle was a British astronomer who coined the term Big Bang.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Fred Hoyle was a 20th-century British astronomer.

clue.text: Mammal in tar pit not completely absorbed

blocks.note: Taken as printed.
Pit without its last letter.

explanation.surface: An animal is partly swallowed up in a tar pit.
explanation.walkthrough: "tar pit" reads as one place where animals get trapped, but tar and pit are separate words, one swallowing the other.
explanation.definitionFit: The tapir is a pig-like mammal with a short trunk.

clue.text: Chapel area in gold colour with blue?

blocks.note: Or is gold in heraldry.
A is the abbreviation for area.
Blue is the colour of the Conservative Party, so a blue is a Tory.

explanation.surface: Part of a chapel decorated in gold and blue.
explanation.walkthrough: Blue as Tory is British political shorthand: the Conservatives' colour is blue.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratory is a small chapel for private prayer.

clue.text: Assign a parking place

blocks.note: Taken as printed.
P is the sign for parking.
A place or spot is a point.

explanation.surface: An instruction to allocate someone a parking space.
explanation.walkthrough: "Assign a parking place" reads as one task, but the definition is "Assign" alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: naming someone to a post, or fixing a time, is allotting it.

clue.text: Article uncovered hate facing mostly left-wing arts arena

indicators.note: Mostly means all but the last letter.

blocks.note: The is the definite article.
Hate without its first and last letters.
Left-wing is red, docked to RE.

explanation.surface: An article exposes the hatred facing a largely left-wing arts venue.
explanation.walkthrough: Red is the colour of the political left, so left-wing is red before it is shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: a playhouse is one kind of venue for the performing arts.

clue.text: Island in unsettled US area, or continental one?

indicators.note: Unsettled letters are not in their places.

blocks.note: The anagram fodder, taken as printed.
I is the abbreviation for island.

explanation.surface: Asking whether some land is an island in an unsettled part of America or a continent.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the clue's own island: rather than an island, EURASIA is a continental landmass, as the question mark admits.
explanation.definitionFit: Eurasia is the combined landmass of Europe and Asia, a continent.
